{{Short description|Mathematical formula}}
In mathematics, the '''Weyl integration formula''', introduced by [[Hermann Weyl]], is an [[integration (mathematics)|integration]] formula for a compact connected [[Lie group]] ''G'' in terms of a [[maximal torus]] ''T''. Precisely, it says<ref>{{harvnb|Adams|1982|loc=Theorem 6.1.}}</ref> there exists a real-valued continuous function ''u'' on ''T'' such that for every [[class function]] ''f'' on ''G'' (function invariant under conjugation by <math>G</math>):
:<math>\int_G f(g) \, dg = \int_T f(t) u(t) \, dt.</math>
Moreover, <math>u</math> is explicitly given as: <math>u = |\delta |^2 / \# W</math> where <math>W = N_G(T)/T</math> is the [[Weyl group]] determined by ''T'' and
:<math>\delta(t) = \prod_{\alpha > 0} \left( e^{\alpha(t)/2} - e^{-\alpha(t)/2} \right),</math>
the product running over the positive roots of ''G'' relative to ''T''. More generally, if <math>f</math> is an arbitrary integrable function, then 
:<math>\int_G f(g) \, dg = \int_T \left( \int_{G/T} f(gtg^{-1}) \, d(gT) \right) u(t) \, dt.</math>
Note that the inner integral is over the manifold <math>G/T</math>, the quotient of the group <math>G</math> over the maximal torus <math>T</math>, and <math>d(gT)</math> is some [[Borel measure]] on this manifold.<ref>Zhang 2014</ref>

The formula can be used to derive the [[Weyl character formula]]. (The theory of [[Verma module]]s, on the other hand, gives a purely algebraic derivation of the Weyl character formula.)

== Derivation ==
Consider the map
:<math>q : G/T \times T \to G, \, (gT, t) \mapsto gtg^{-1}</math>.
The Weyl group ''W'' acts on ''T'' by conjugation and on <math>G/T</math> from the left by: for <math>nT \in W</math>,
:<math>nT(gT) = gn^{-1} T.</math>
Let <math>G/T \times_W T</math> be the quotient space by this ''W''-action. Then, since the ''W''-action on <math>G/T</math> is free, the quotient map
:<math>p: G/T \times T \to G/T \times_W T</math>
is a smooth covering with fiber ''W'' when it is restricted to regular points. Now, <math>q</math> is <math>p</math> followed by <math>G/T \times_W T \to G</math> and the latter is a [[homeomorphism]] on regular points and so has degree one. Hence, the degree of <math>q</math> is <math>\# W</math> and, by the change of variable formula,<!-- TODO: an internal link to a relevant article. --> we get:
:<math>\# W \int_G f \, dg = \int_{G/T \times T} q^*(f \, dg).</math>
Here, <math>q^*(f \, dg)|_{(gT, t)} = f(t) q^*(dg)|_{(gT, t)}</math> since <math>f</math> is a class function. We next compute <math>q^*(dg)|_{(gT, t)}</math>. We identify a [[tangent space]] to <math>G/T \times T</math> as <math>\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t} \oplus \mathfrak{t}</math> where <math>\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{t}</math> are the Lie algebras of <math>G, T</math>. For each <math>v \in T</math>,
:<math>q(gv, t) = gvtv^{-1}g^{-1}</math>
and thus, on <math>\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t}</math>, we have:
:<math>d(gT \mapsto q(gT, t))(\dot v) = gtg^{-1}(gt^{-1} \dot v t g^{-1} - g \dot v g^{-1}) = (\operatorname{Ad}(g) \circ (\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-1}) - I))(\dot v).</math>
Similarly we see, on <math>\mathfrak{t}</math>, <math>d(t \mapsto q(gT, t)) = \operatorname{Ad}(g)</math>. Now, we can view ''G'' as a connected subgroup of an [[orthogonal group]] (as it is compact connected) and thus <math>\det(\operatorname{Ad}(g)) = 1</math>. Hence,
:<math>q^*(dg) = \det(\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t}}(t^{-1}) - I_{\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t}})\, dg.</math>
To compute the [[determinant]], we recall that <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}} = \mathfrak{t}_{\mathbb{C}} \oplus \bigoplus_\alpha \mathfrak{g}_\alpha</math> where <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\alpha} = \{ x \in \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}} \mid \operatorname{Ad}(t) x = e^{\alpha(t)} x, t \in T \}</math> and each <math>\mathfrak{g}_\alpha</math> has dimension one. Hence, considering the eigenvalues of <math>\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t}}(t^{-1})</math>, we get:
:<math>\det(\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t}}(t^{-1}) - I_{\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t}}) = \prod_{\alpha > 0} (e^{-\alpha(t)} - 1)(e^{\alpha(t)} - 1) = \delta(t) \overline{\delta(t)},</math>
as each root <math>\alpha</math> has pure imaginary value.

== Weyl character formula ==
{{expand section|date=April 2020}}<!-- This section is incomplete. -->
{{main|Weyl character formula}}

The Weyl character formula is a consequence of the [[Weyl integral]] formula as follows. We first note that <math>W</math> can be identified with a subgroup of <math>\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak{t}_{\mathbb{C}}^*)</math>; in particular, it acts on the set of roots, linear functionals on <math>\mathfrak{t}_{\mathbb{C}}</math>. Let
:<math>A_{\mu} = \sum_{w \in W} (-1)^{l(w)} e^{w(\mu)}</math>
where <math>l(w)</math> is the [[length of a Weyl group element|length]] of ''w''. Let <math>\Lambda</math> be the [[weight lattice]] of ''G'' relative to ''T''. The Weyl character formula then says that: for each irreducible character <math>\chi</math> of <math>G</math>, there exists a <math>\mu \in \Lambda</math> such that
:<math>\chi|T \cdot \delta = A_{\mu}</math>.
To see this, we first note
# <math>\|\chi \|^2 = \int_G |\chi|^2 dg = 1.</math>
# <math>\chi|T \cdot \delta \in \mathbb{Z}[\Lambda].</math>
The property (1) is precisely (a part of) the [[orthogonality relation]]s on irreducible characters.
